question:
Select the option with the correct use of article(s).
William Wordsworth was ___ romantic poet. He did things in ___ unusual manner.
option_1: William Wordsworth was a romantic poet. He did things in an unusual manner.
option_2: William Wordsworth was romantic poet. He did things in an unusual manner.
option_3: William Wordsworth was the romantic poet. He did things in a unusual manner.
option_4: William Wordsworth was a romantic poet. He did things in a unusual manner.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. William Wordsworth was a romantic poet. He did things in an unusual manner.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule 1 — "a" vs "an": The article "a" is used before words beginning with a consonant sound, and "an" is used before words beginning with a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u sound), not necessarily a vowel letter.

• "Romantic" begins with the consonant sound /r/, so it takes the article "a" → "a romantic poet."

• "Unusual" begins with the vowel sound /ʌ/ (as in "umbrella"), even though it starts with the letter "u", so it takes the article "an" → "an unusual manner."
◦ Compare: words like "university" or "uniform" start with the consonant sound /j/ ("yoo"), so they take "a" (a university, a uniform) — but "unusual" does NOT have this /j/ sound.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because the singular countable noun "poet" cannot stand without an article — it needs "a" before it ("a romantic poet").

• Option 3 is incorrect because "the romantic poet" wrongly uses the definite article (no specific, previously-mentioned poet is being pointed to), and "a unusual manner" wrongly uses "a" before a vowel sound instead of "an".

• Option 4 is incorrect because "a unusual manner" wrongly uses "a" before the vowel sound of "unusual"; it should be "an unusual manner".

NOTE

• Words like "hour", "honest", "heir", "honour" take "an" because the initial "h" is silent (an hour, an honest man).

• Words like "university", "union", "European", "one-eyed", "useful" take "a" because they begin with the consonant sound /j/ or /w/, despite starting with a vowel letter.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The manager noticed / that Pragya / was first to reach / the office on Saturday.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. was first to reach.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "was first to reach" is missing the definite article "the" before the superlative-like ordinal "first". It should read "was the first to reach."

• Rule: When "first", "second", "last", "only", etc. are used to single out one person/thing out of a group, they must be preceded by the definite article "the" — e.g., "He was the first to arrive", not "He was first to arrive" (in formal written English, the article is required before such an ordinal used as a noun-phrase head).

• Corrected sentence: "The manager noticed that Pragya was the first to reach the office on Saturday."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "that Pragya" is correct — it correctly introduces the noun clause (object of "noticed") with the subordinating conjunction "that".

• Option 2: "The manager noticed" is correct — subject "The manager" agrees with the singular verb "noticed" in the simple past tense.

• Option 4: "the office on Saturday" is correct — the definite article "the" is correctly used before the specific noun "office", and "on Saturday" is the correct preposition for a day.

NOTE

• Similar constructions requiring "the": "the best", "the last one to leave", "the only student to pass".

• Do not confuse this with adverbial use of "first" (e.g., "He first went home"), where no article is needed because "first" functions as an adverb, not as a noun phrase referring to a specific person.

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
The chief guest gave out prizes to the meritorious students of the school.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. gave out prizes.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "gave out prizes" uses the wrong phrasal verb. The standard, idiomatic collocation for distributing prizes/awards at a function is "give away prizes", not "give out prizes".

• "Give out" generally means to distribute something in general (leaflets, information) or to become exhausted/stop working ("his patience gave out"), whereas "give away" is specifically the standard usage for handing out prizes, gifts, or awards ceremonially.

• Corrected sentence: "The chief guest gave away prizes to the meritorious students of the school."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "of the school" is correct — it correctly modifies "the meritorious students", showing which students are meant.

• Option 3: "to the meritorious students" is correct — "to" is the correct preposition to introduce the indirect object/recipient.

• Option 4: "The chief guest" is correct — a grammatically sound subject noun phrase with the correct article "the".

NOTE

• Common exam confusions with phrasal verbs of similar form: give away (distribute/donate/betray a secret), give up (quit), give in (surrender), give out (distribute widely/run out), give off (emit, e.g. a smell).

• Related exam phrase: a school function where prizes are distributed is called a "prize-giving ceremony" or "prize distribution ceremony".

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
Mathematics help/ in developing/ the logical mindset /of students.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Mathematics help.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Mathematics" is one of a group of nouns that end in "-s" but are treated as singular, uncountable nouns (they name a single subject/discipline). Such nouns always take a singular verb.

• Rule: Subject-verb agreement requires "Mathematics" + singular verb → "Mathematics helps", not "Mathematics help".

• Corrected sentence: "Mathematics helps in developing the logical mindset of students."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "in developing" is correct — the gerund correctly follows the preposition "in".

• Option 2: "the logical mindset" is correct — a grammatically sound noun phrase functioning as the object of "developing".

• Option 4: "of students" is correct — "of" correctly shows possession/association with "mindset".

NOTE

• Other subjects/nouns ending in "-s" but taking a singular verb: Physics, Economics, Statistics, Civics, Ethics, News, Measles, Mumps, Innings, Billiards (e.g., "Physics is an interesting subject", "The news is good").

• Contrast with nouns that look singular but are always plural and take a plural verb: scissors, trousers, spectacles, people (in the sense of persons), cattle — these are treated the opposite way.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 1.

Water is 1.________ for life and for good health. Not only is it necessary for us to be able to meet our daily needs but safe drinking water can 2._____ many water-related diseases. India has one of the largest number of cases of 3._____ such as diarrhoea, dysentery, and cholera. Over 1,600 Indians, most of them children below the age of five, 4.________ die every day because of water-related diseases. These deaths can be prevented if people have 5._______ to safe drinking water.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. essential.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Essential" means absolutely necessary or extremely important; it fits perfectly with the passage's idea that water is a basic necessity "for life and for good health."

• The next sentence reinforces this — "it is necessary for us to be able to meet our daily needs" — which is a paraphrase of "essential", confirming the contextual fit.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "primary" means first in order of importance or occurring first; it does not convey the sense of indispensability that the sentence needs.

• Option 3: "intrinsic" means belonging naturally to something as an essential characteristic, referring to an inherent internal quality — it does not fit the idea of water being necessary for an outcome (life/health).

• Option 4: "insistent" means demanding attention persistently; it is unrelated in meaning to necessity and does not fit the context at all.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always check the sentence both before and after the blank — the surrounding context ("necessary for us to be able to meet our daily needs") often paraphrases or hints at the exact word needed.

• Words related to "essential": indispensable, vital, crucial, imperative, requisite.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 2.

Water is 1.________ for life and for good health. Not only is it necessary for us to be able to meet our daily needs but safe drinking water can 2._____ many water-related diseases. India has one of the largest number of cases of 3._____ such as diarrhoea, dysentery, and cholera. Over 1,600 Indians, most of them children below the age of five, 4.________ die every day because of water-related diseases. These deaths can be prevented if people have 5._______ to safe drinking water.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. prevent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Prevent" means to stop something (especially something undesirable, like a disease) from happening. Safe drinking water can prevent water-related diseases such as diarrhoea, dysentery, and cholera — this fits the context precisely.

• The following sentence about "cases of diseases" confirms that the passage is talking about safe water stopping diseases from occurring, not restraining people or forbidding an action.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "forbid" means to order someone not to do something; it applies to people's actions/behaviour, not to diseases, so it is contextually wrong.

• Option 3: "restrain" means to hold someone or something back physically or forcefully (e.g., restrain a person); it is not the natural collocation with "diseases".

• Option 4: "hamper" means to hinder or slow down progress; it does not mean to stop a disease from occurring altogether, so it is weaker and contextually inappropriate here.

NOTE

• "Prevent" typically collocates with diseases, accidents, crime, disasters (e.g., "prevent an accident", "prevent the spread of disease").

• "Restrain" collocates with people/emotions/impulses (restrain oneself, restrain anger); "forbid" collocates with actions/permissions (forbid entry).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 3.

Water is 1.________ for life and for good health. Not only is it necessary for us to be able to meet our daily needs but safe drinking water can 2._____ many water-related diseases. India has one of the largest number of cases of 3._____ such as diarrhoea, dysentery, and cholera. Over 1,600 Indians, most of them children below the age of five, 4.________ die every day because of water-related diseases. These deaths can be prevented if people have 5._______ to safe drinking water.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. diseases.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank is immediately followed by the examples "such as diarrhoea, dysentery, and cholera", all of which are specific names of diseases. The word that fits must be a general category term for these examples.

• "Cases of diseases" is also a natural, commonly used collocation in medical/statistical contexts ("India has one of the largest number of cases of diseases such as...").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "distress" means suffering or anxiety; diarrhoea, dysentery, and cholera are not examples of "distress", they are named diseases, so this does not fit.

• Option 3: "laments" means expressions of grief or sorrow; it does not make sense as a category that includes diarrhoea, dysentery, and cholera.

• Option 4: "sufferings" is too general/abstract a noun to be exemplified specifically by named illnesses like diarrhoea, dysentery, and cholera; "diseases" is the precise, natural fit.

NOTE

• When a blank is followed by "such as" + a list of specific items, the correct word is almost always the general category/class name that those items belong to.

• Common water-borne diseases for SSC GK/vocabulary overlap: diarrhoea, dysentery, cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A, jaundice.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 4.

Water is 1.________ for life and for good health. Not only is it necessary for us to be able to meet our daily needs but safe drinking water can 2._____ many water-related diseases. India has one of the largest number of cases of 3._____ such as diarrhoea, dysentery, and cholera. Over 1,600 Indians, most of them children below the age of five, 4.________ die every day because of water-related diseases. These deaths can be prevented if people have 5._______ to safe drinking water.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. reportedly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Reportedly" means according to what is said or reported (i.e., based on reports/statistics), which fits perfectly with a passage citing a statistic ("Over 1,600 Indians... die every day") that is presented as reported data/information, not as the writer's own direct observation.

• The sentence is presenting a statistical claim, and "reportedly" is the standard adverb used to introduce information sourced from reports, exactly the tone of this passage.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "distinctly" means clearly or in a way that is easy to perceive; it does not fit the sense of citing reported/statistical information.

• Option 2: "assuredly" means with confidence or certainty; it implies the writer's personal certainty rather than reported data, which does not match the context.

• Option 4: "ostensibly" means apparently or seemingly (as opposed to what is actually true), which introduces a doubt/contrast not present in this straightforward factual statement.

NOTE

• "Reportedly" is commonly used in news/statistical writing to attribute a claim to a source without the writer vouching for it personally.

• Do not confuse "reportedly" (according to reports) with "allegedly" (according to unproven claims/accusations) or "apparently/ostensibly" (seemingly, but perhaps not actually true).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 5.

Water is 1.________ for life and for good health. Not only is it necessary for us to be able to meet our daily needs but safe drinking water can 2._____ many water-related diseases. India has one of the largest number of cases of 3._____ such as diarrhoea, dysentery, and cholera. Over 1,600 Indians, most of them children below the age of five, 4.________ die every day because of water-related diseases. These deaths can be prevented if people have 5._______ to safe drinking water.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. access.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Access" means the means or opportunity to obtain or make use of something. The standard collocation "have access to (safe drinking water)" is exactly the phrase used in public health/development writing.

• The sentence "These deaths can be prevented if people have _____ to safe drinking water" needs a noun that pairs with "have... to", and "access to" is the fixed, natural collocation.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "entrance" means a way into a physical place (a door/gate) or the act of entering; it does not collocate with "have ___ to safe drinking water".

• Option 3: "providence" means divine care/foresight or God's guidance; it is unrelated in meaning and does not fit grammatically with "have ___ to".

• Option 4: "accession" means the act of formally taking up a position (e.g., accession to the throne) or a country joining a treaty; it does not fit the sense of "having access to" a resource.

NOTE

• "Access to" is a very common SSC/UPSC vocabulary collocation, seen in phrases like "access to education", "access to healthcare", "access to clean water".

• Do not confuse access (means of obtaining/using) with excess (too much of something) — they are commonly confused in spelling-based questions too.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the following sentence.
Had you been to Dubai, I would also go with you.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. I would have gone.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence begins with "Had you been to Dubai," which is an inverted form of the if-clause of the Third Conditional (unreal/hypothetical situation in the past): "If you had been to Dubai, ..."

• Rule — Third Conditional (Type 3):
◦ If-clause: If + subject + had + V3
◦ Main clause: subject + would/could/might + have + V3

• Applying the rule, the main clause must be "I would have gone with you" — the base form "go" changes to the past participle "gone", preceded by "would have".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "I shall be gone" is incorrect — "shall be gone" is a future/passive-like form, not the required "would have + V3" structure for a Third Conditional main clause.

• Option 2: "I will have went" is incorrect on two counts — "will" cannot follow a past-unreal if-clause, and "have went" is grammatically wrong (the past participle of "go" is "gone", not "went").

• Option 3: "I would has also gone" is incorrect because after the modal "would", the base form "have" must be used, not "has" (modals are always followed by the base form of the next verb).

NOTE

• Third Conditional sentences talk about an imaginary/impossible past situation and its imagined past result — e.g., "If I had studied harder, I would have passed."

• After any modal verb (would, could, should, might, must, will, can), the following verb is always in its base form (e.g., would have, not would has; would go, not would goes).

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Costing an arm and a leg
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Very costly and luxurious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to cost an arm and a leg" means to be extremely expensive, so costly that it feels as if one is sacrificing something as valuable as a limb to pay for it. (बहुत महँगा होना)
◦ Example: That designer handbag cost her an arm and a leg.

• The idiom likely originates from the idea that losing an arm or a leg would be an enormous, almost unbearable price to pay — used figuratively for something very costly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Very attractive and cheap" is the opposite meaning; the idiom refers to something being very expensive, not cheap.

• Option 2: "Very rough and tough" is unrelated to cost or price and does not match the idiom's meaning.

• Option 4: "Very entertaining and jovial" describes a mood or personality, not a price, and is unrelated to this idiom.

NOTE

• Other SSC idioms about being expensive: "a king's ransom" (राजाओं जैसी कीमत, an extremely large sum), "burn a hole in one's pocket" (जेब खाली कर देना, to be very expensive/costly to buy), "steep price" (बहुत ऊँची कीमत).

• Idioms of the opposite sense (cheap): "dirt cheap", "for a song" (both mean very inexpensive).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word given in brackets to fill in the blank.
You can't stop the _________ (outflow) of current.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. influx.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Influx" means the arrival or flowing in of people or things in large numbers; it means an inward flow, which is the exact opposite of "outflow" (an outward flow). (अंतर्वाह/भीतर आना)
◦ Example: The city saw a huge influx of tourists during the festival.

• Outflow = flowing OUT; Influx = flowing IN — these are direct antonyms based on direction.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "deluge" (बाढ़, जलप्लावन): means a severe flood or an overwhelming rush of something; it describes intensity, not direction, and is not an antonym of "outflow".

• Option 3: "torrent" (तेज़ धारा): means a strong, fast-moving stream; again a synonym-type word describing forceful flow, not the opposite of "outflow".

• Option 4: "income": relates to money earned, not a flow of current/liquid, so it is not a valid antonym in this physical-flow context.

NOTE

• Common outflow/influx-type antonym pairs tested by SSC: inflow ↔ outflow, import ↔ export, ingress ↔ egress, inhale ↔ exhale.

• "Influx" is frequently used for migration/tourism contexts ("an influx of refugees"), while "outflow" is used for capital, water, or population leaving a place.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Massive
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Tiny.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Massive" means extremely large in size, extent, or amount. (विशाल)
◦ Example: The company suffered massive losses this year.

• "Tiny" means extremely small in size. (बहुत छोटा) It is the direct opposite of "massive" on the scale of size.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Tall" (लंबा): describes height, which is a near-synonym dimension of largeness, not its opposite.

• Option 3: "Formidable" (दुर्जेय, प्रभावशाली): means inspiring fear or respect through being impressively large, powerful, or capable — this is close in meaning to "massive", not its opposite.

• Option 4: "Heavy" (भारी): describes weight, which is a related but synonymous quality often associated with "massive", not its antonym.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "massive": huge, enormous, colossal, immense, gigantic, vast.

• Other antonyms of size-related words often tested: enormous ↔ minuscule, gigantic ↔ minute, huge ↔ diminutive.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the given sentence.
She argued against the unnecessary split in the committee.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. division.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Split", in this context, means a division or separation into factions/parts (e.g., a split within a committee/party). (विभाजन)
◦ Example: The split in the party led to the formation of two rival groups.

• "Division" carries the same meaning of separation into opposing parts/factions, making it the correct substitute for "split" in this sentence. (विभाजन)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "blend" (मिश्रण): means a smooth mixture of different things; this is nearly the opposite of "split" (which implies separation, not mixing).

• Option 3: "combination" (संयोजन): means the joining together of things; this contradicts the sense of "split", which means coming apart, not joining.

• Option 4: "mix" (मिश्रण): similarly implies combining different elements together, which is the opposite idea to a "split"/division.

NOTE

• "Split" can mean either a physical crack/tear (the log split in two) or, as here, a division of opinion/faction within a group — always check context.

• Synonyms of "split" (in the division sense): rift, schism, breach, rupture, divide.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the following sentence.
This serum contains ingredients enabling the hair to grow.
option_4: that enable the hair to grow
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. that enable the hair to grow.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment "enabling the hair to grow" is a present-participle phrase modifying "ingredients". It can be correctly rewritten as a relative clause: "that enable the hair to grow", keeping the same meaning and correct grammar.

• Rule: A present participle phrase modifying a plural noun ("ingredients") can be replaced by a relative pronoun ("that"/"which") + a plural verb agreeing with that noun: "ingredients that enable..." (enable, not enables, to agree with plural "ingredients").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "the enable grow hair" is grammatically broken — "enable" and "grow" cannot be strung together as bare verb forms like this; it does not form a coherent noun/verb phrase.

• Option 2: "for growth hair" is incorrect word order and usage — it should be "for hair growth" if a noun phrase were intended, and even then it loses the sense of "enabling" (making it possible).

• Option 3: "for growing many hair" is incorrect because "hair" (referring to hair in general, on the head) is an uncountable noun and cannot be quantified with "many"; it should be "more hair" or simply "hair growth", not "many hair".

NOTE

• "Hair" is uncountable when referring to the mass of hair on one's head ("her hair is long") but countable when referring to individual strands ("there's a hair in my soup", "three grey hairs").

• Present participle phrases (V-ing) modifying a noun can usually be converted to a relative clause: "that/which" + a verb agreeing with the noun in number and tense.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Neice (correct spelling: Niece).

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Niece" — the daughter of one's brother or sister.

• Spelling key: it follows the common English rule "i before e, except after c" — since there is no "c" immediately before this vowel pair, the correct order is "ie", not "ei": N-I-E-C-E.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Dilemma" is spelt correctly — a situation requiring a choice between equally undesirable alternatives.

• Option 2: "Committee" is spelt correctly — note the double "m" and double "t" and double "e" (com-mit-tee).

• Option 3: "Warranty" is spelt correctly — a written guarantee.

NOTE

• "i before e except after c" examples: believe, achieve, niece, piece (ie) vs. receive, ceiling, deceive (ei after c).

• Common exceptions to this rule (worth memorising for spelling questions): weird, seize, either, neither, height, foreign, science.

question:
Select the word segment from the options that can substitute the bracketed word segment meaningfully.
Telangana artists (are know for the amazing bronze castings).
option_1: Are known for their amazing bronze castings
option_2: Have been knew to the amazing bronze castings
option_3: Is known to the amazing bronze castings
option_4: Have to know the amazing bronze castings
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Are known for their amazing bronze castings.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The original bracketed segment "are know for" is grammatically wrong — "know" is a base form and cannot follow "are" directly in a passive-voice-like descriptive sense; the correct passive/adjectival form is "are known for" (be + past participle).

• Rule: The fixed expression to describe what someone is famous/recognised for is "be known for + noun/gerund" (e.g., "She is known for her honesty"). The plural subject "Telangana artists" needs the plural auxiliary "are".

• The possessive "their" correctly replaces "the" before "amazing bronze castings" to show that the castings belong to/are made by the artists.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Have been knew to" is incorrect — "knew" is the simple past form and cannot be used after "have been" (which requires a past participle, "known"); also "known to" (rather than "for") changes the correct collocation.

• Option 3: "Is known to" is incorrect — the subject "Telangana artists" is plural and requires "are", not "is"; also, "known to" is the wrong preposition (should be "known for" when describing a reputation/skill).

• Option 4: "Have to know" is incorrect — this changes the meaning entirely to an obligation ("must know") rather than describing a reputation/fame, which is not the intended meaning.

NOTE

• Fixed collocations: "known for" (famous because of a quality/skill), "known to" (familiar to a person, e.g., "This fact is known to me").

• Always check subject-verb agreement (singular/plural) when a sentence's subject and its auxiliary verb are separated by other words.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.
It has been found that the trees are being destroyed by a moth.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. No substitution required.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The original sentence is already grammatically correct: "the trees are being destroyed by a moth" is the correct Passive Voice, Present Continuous Tense form.

• Rule — Present Continuous Passive: Subject (plural) + are being + V3 + by + agent. Since "trees" is plural, the auxiliary "are" correctly agrees with it, and "being destroyed" is the correct passive continuous form.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "have destroyed" is incorrect — this is Present Perfect Active voice, which changes both the tense and voice, and would wrongly make "trees" the doer rather than the receiver of the action.

• Option 2: "is being destroyed" is incorrect — "is" is the singular auxiliary, but the subject "trees" is plural, so it should be "are being destroyed", not "is being destroyed" — this creates a subject-verb agreement error.

• Option 3: "have been destroying" is incorrect — this is Present Perfect Continuous Active voice (implying the trees are the ones destroying something), which reverses the intended passive meaning.

NOTE

• Always check whether the original underlined portion is already correct before assuming a substitution is required — SSC frequently includes a "No substitution/improvement required" option as the correct answer.

• Passive voice formula by tense: Present Continuous → is/am/are + being + V3; Present Perfect → has/have + been + V3; Simple Present → is/am/are + V3.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Tom is trying to ____________ as soon as possible.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. get a job.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct, natural collocation in English for finding/obtaining employment is "get a job" (or "find a job"), not "receive", "experience", or "learn" a job.

• Rule — Collocation: Certain verbs pair naturally with certain nouns by convention/usage rather than by strict logical rule; "job" collocates with "get", "find", "land", "take up" — not with "receive", "experience", or "learn".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "receive a job" is incorrect — "receive" is used for something handed/given to you directly (receive a gift, receive a letter), not for obtaining employment through effort.

• Option 2: "experience a job" is incorrect — "experience" collocates with feelings or events (experience joy, experience difficulty), not with the act of obtaining a job.

• Option 4: "learn a job" is incorrect — "learn" refers to acquiring knowledge/skill (learn a language, learn a skill), not to the act of obtaining employment.

NOTE

• Common job-related collocations tested by SSC: get/find/land a job, apply for a job, lose a job, quit a job, look for a job.

• Collocation-based fill-in-the-blank questions are best solved by memorising common fixed verb-noun pairings rather than translating literally.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Going through a sticky patch
option_1: To experience a bad period in life
option_3: To walk on a muddy road
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To experience a bad period in life.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "a sticky patch" (or "a sticky situation/patch") means a difficult or troublesome period or situation. (कठिन/मुश्किल दौर)
◦ Example: The company is going through a sticky patch after losing its biggest client.

• "Sticky" here is used figuratively to mean something one is stuck in and finds hard to get out of — i.e., a difficult phase.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Try to paste something unsuccessfully" takes "sticky" too literally (as an adhesive) and is not the figurative meaning of the idiom.

• Option 3: "To walk on a muddy road" is again a literal misreading of "sticky" (as in mud); it is not the idiomatic sense.

• Option 4: "To feel sad" is too narrow and does not capture the idiom's specific meaning of going through a prolonged difficult situation/period, not just an emotion.

NOTE

• Other idioms about difficult times often tested by SSC: "in hot water" (in trouble), "between a rock and a hard place" (facing two equally difficult choices), "go through a rough patch" (a synonym of "sticky patch"), "through thick and thin" (through good and bad times).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
His feeble opponent was no match to him and ultimately he won the challenge.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Strong.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Feeble" means lacking physical strength or power; weak. (कमज़ोर)
◦ Example: The feeble old man could barely climb the stairs.

• "Strong" means having great physical power or force, which is the direct opposite of "feeble". (मज़बूत/शक्तिशाली)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Mystic" (रहस्यवादी): relates to spiritual or mystical matters; it has no connection to physical strength and is not an antonym of "feeble".

• Option 3: "Major" (प्रमुख/बड़ा): means important or larger in size/rank; it does not specifically describe physical strength as the opposite of "feeble".

• Option 4: "Intelligent" (बुद्धिमान): relates to mental ability, not physical strength, so it cannot be the antonym of "feeble" (which is about physical weakness).

NOTE

• Synonyms of "feeble": weak, frail, fragile, delicate, infirm.

• Other antonym pairs of "weak/feeble" tested by SSC: frail ↔ robust, delicate ↔ sturdy, fragile ↔ tough.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Impulsive
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Cautious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Impulsive" means acting or done suddenly, without careful thought or planning. (आवेगी, बिना सोचे-समझे काम करने वाला)
◦ Example: He made an impulsive decision to quit his job without planning ahead.

• "Cautious" means careful to avoid potential problems or dangers, i.e., acting only after careful thought — the direct opposite of acting impulsively. (सावधान, सतर्क)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Passive" (निष्क्रिय): means not taking an active role, accepting things without resistance; this is a different trait from being careful/thoughtful, and is not a true antonym of "impulsive".

• Option 2: "Aggressive" (आक्रामक): means ready to attack or confront; this is actually closer in spirit to "impulsive" (both involve acting forcefully) rather than being its opposite.

• Option 3: "Hasty" (जल्दबाज़ी वाला): is in fact a near-synonym of "impulsive" (acting with excessive speed/without thought), not its antonym.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "impulsive": hasty, rash, spontaneous, reckless, impetuous.

• Other antonym pairs tested by SSC: rash ↔ prudent, reckless ↔ careful, impetuous ↔ deliberate.

question:
Identify the incorrectly spelt word and select its correct spelling.
There are a number of artists currently creating unique, collectble teapots.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. collectable.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word printed in the sentence, "collectble", is misspelt — it is missing a vowel. The correct spelling is "collectable" (an acceptable variant of "collectible"), meaning an item worth collecting as a hobby.

• Spelling key: COLLECT + ABLE — the base word "collect" plus the suffix "-able" (denoting "capable of being ___"), giving "collectable".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "currantly" is incorrect — this misspells "currently" (mixing it up with "currant", a dried fruit); the correct word would be "currently", but this is not the word being tested ("collectble" is).

• Option 3: "collectibile" is incorrect — this is a wrong spelling of "collectible", with an extra, misplaced "i".

• Option 4: "currintly" is incorrect — another misspelling of "currently", with the wrong vowel "i" instead of "e".

NOTE

• Both "collectable" and "collectible" are accepted spellings in English, but only the option matching the exact correction expected ("collectable") is treated as correct in this question.

• Similar "-able"/"-ible" suffix confusions common in spelling questions: "accessible" vs "washable", "responsible" vs "comfortable", "visible" vs "reliable" — there is no fixed rule, so these must be memorised individually.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word 'Commence' from the given sentence.
Let's put an end to this discussion about voodoo and instead talk about something amusing.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. end.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Commence" means to begin or start something. (आरंभ करना)
◦ Example: The ceremony will commence at 9 a.m.

• "End" means to bring or come to a finish/conclusion, which is the direct opposite of "commence" (to begin). (समाप्त करना/अंत)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "voodoo" is simply the topic being discussed in the sentence; it has no meaning relationship to "commence" at all.

• Option 3: "amusing" means entertaining or funny; it describes a quality of the new topic, not an antonym of "begin".

• Option 4: "discussion" is a noun referring to the conversation itself; it is not an antonym of the verb "commence".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "commence": begin, start, initiate, launch, inaugurate.

• Other antonym pairs of "commence"/"begin" tested by SSC: initiate ↔ terminate, launch ↔ conclude, start ↔ finish/cease.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Evasive
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Ambiguous.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Evasive" means tending to avoid giving a direct or clear answer, often deliberately unclear or non-committal. (टालमटोल करने वाला, अस्पष्ट)
◦ Example: The minister gave an evasive reply when asked about the scandal.

• "Ambiguous" means open to more than one interpretation, unclear or vague in meaning — closely matching the sense of deliberately unclear/non-committal speech conveyed by "evasive". (अस्पष्ट, दुविधापूर्ण)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Cohesive" (सुसंगत): means forming a united whole, well-integrated; this is essentially opposite in spirit to "evasive" (which implies avoiding clarity/commitment), not a synonym.

• Option 3: "Accessible" (सुलभ): means easy to approach, reach, or understand; this is nearly opposite to "evasive", which implies being hard to pin down.

• Option 4: "Abrasive" (कर्कश, रूखा): means harsh or rough in manner; it describes a manner of speaking/behaving, unrelated to the sense of avoiding directness conveyed by "evasive".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "evasive": vague, elusive, non-committal, equivocal, cagey.

• Do not confuse "evasive" (avoiding a direct answer) with "elusive" (hard to find/catch) — the two are related but used in slightly different contexts, both frequently tested by SSC.
